meta.title: Navajo Alphabet and Sounds
meta.subtitle: 41 letters and sounds · both directions, as two cards per letter
meta.desc: The Latin alphabet in which Navajo (Diné bizaad) is written: 41 notes, one per letter or digraph in the order of the standard orthography (Young and Morgan's, of 1937–1940), then the four things it marks on a vowel and the n that stands as a syllable. The first deck of the Navajo collection. Both directions: see a letter and recall its sound, or see a sound and recall the letter, each a card with its own schedule. The letters that matter are the ones an English reader would misread: b, d, g, j and dz are said WITHOUT the puff of air English gives p, t, k, ch and ts, while t, k, ch and ts have a strong one, t and k often a rasp; the EJECTIVES tʼ, kʼ, chʼ, tsʼ and tłʼ are said with the throat shut and a burst of air pushed out; ł is a voiceless l, like the Welsh ll; gh is a soft sound at the back of the mouth; and the apostrophe ʼ is a consonant, the glottal stop. On the vowels, ordinary Navajo writing marks a LONG vowel by doubling it (aa), a HIGH TONE with an acute accent (á; a low tone is unmarked), a NASAL vowel with a hook beneath it (ą), and the falling and rising tones of a long vowel (áa, aá). Each card gives one everyday word that shows the sound, from the Navajo A1 lexicon, with its pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet as English Wiktionary gives it. The sounds are approximations, as every learner's alphabet gives them. There is no read-aloud button: no device carries a Navajo voice, and one without it reads the letter in English. Sources: Wikipedia, 'Navajo phonology' and 'Navajo language' (orthography), read 2026-11-16, which follow McDonough (2003) and Young and Morgan (1987); the example words and their IPA are English Wiktionary's, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0).

fields.Sound: the GLOTTAL STOP, the catch in the middle of uh-oh — a letter of its own, written inside a word or at its end; a word that seems to begin with a vowel starts with one, unwritten
the a of father
a p without the puff of air English puts after it — to an English ear between b and p, never a buzzing b
the ch of church, with a strong puff of air
an EJECTIVE ch: the throat is shut and a burst of air is pushed out with the ch, giving a sharp popping sound — a different letter from ch
a t without the puff of air — to an English ear between d and t
a t without the puff, released at once through the sides of the tongue into a short l — one sound, not d followed by l
a ts without the puff of air — to an English ear close to the ds of beds
short, the e of bet; doubled (ee), longer and closer to the e of café
a k without the puff of air — to an English ear between g and k
a soft sound made at the back of the mouth, between a gargled g and a w — before o it is nearly a w
the h of hat; at the end of a syllable it is rougher, like the ch of Scottish loch
h said with rounded lips, like a breathy wh
short, the i of bit; doubled (ii), longer and higher — never the i of kite
a ch without the puff of air — to an English ear close to the j of jam
a k with a strong puff of air, often a rasp like k followed by the ch of loch
an EJECTIVE k: the throat is shut and a burst of air is pushed out, a sharp popping k — a different letter from k
the rasping k with rounded lips, as in the qu of queen
the l of let
a VOICELESS l: breath hissed past the sides of the tongue with no voice, like the Welsh ll of Llanelli
the m of man; found in only a few Navajo words
the n of no; it can also stand as a syllable of its own and carry a tone (ń, below)
the o of so, said pure; Navajo has no u, and o never drifts to one
the s of sun
the sh of shop, with the lips not rounded
a t with a strong puff of air, often a rasp like t followed by the ch of loch
an EJECTIVE t: the throat is shut and a burst of air is pushed out, a sharp popping t — a different letter from t
a t released at once into the voiceless ł, with a puff of air — one sound
an EJECTIVE tł: the throat shut, the t released into ł with a pop
the ts of cats, with a puff of air — one sound
an EJECTIVE ts: the throat shut, a sharp popping ts — a different letter from ts
the w of we
the ch of Scottish loch, a rasp at the back of the mouth; written x in a few words, mostly after s
the y of yes
the z of zoo, often with little voice
the s of measure
a LONG vowel, written doubled and held about twice as long; length alone can tell two words apart
a HIGH TONE, marked with an acute accent and said on a higher pitch; a vowel with no mark has a low tone
a FALLING tone (áa) or a RISING tone (aá) across a long vowel — found mostly in contractions and in loanwords
a NASAL vowel, marked with a hook beneath it and said partly through the nose, as in French; it can also carry a high tone (ą́)
n standing as a syllable of its own, here with a high tone
